# Abstract {-}

Extreme weather is increasing in frequency and severity due to climate change, thus straining global healthcare systems. Predicting weather-induced healthcare demand in a changing climate will be crucial in achieving Sustainable Development Goal 3 for ensuring healthy lives. Existing evidence indicates that extreme temperatures, rainfall and storms adversely affect mortality and morbidity rates across diseases, population groups and contexts. However, existing models are not readily accessible or granular enough for healthcare providers to use for hospital-level forecasts and decision-making. This project will apply novel, specialized time series models to capture sub-regional variation of weather-related hospital admissions in the UK and India. The models will incorporate weather predictions and extremes, providing hospital admission forecasts at the level of condition, demographics, and geography over a one- to two-week period. The UK and India were chosen to illustrate differences in defining weather extremes between climates and associated model considerations. By improving the predictive accuracy of these patterns—specifically the timing and extent of their peaks—the project aims to inform operational responses to mitigate weather-induced strain on healthcare systems under different climate change scenarios.

## Summary {.unlisted .unnumbered}

Section 1 will introduce the motivation and methodological challenges of forecsting climate-related health research. Section 2 will demonstrate benefits and limitations of current state-of the-art models (`dnlm`) in climate-health research. Section 3 aims to provide an comprehensive breakdown of new growth curve time series models (`tsgc`) for univariate predictions, using COVID-19 cases as a case study. Section 4 will adapt tsgc to handle multiple variables, including weather exposures and demographic controls.
